events.title: JavaScript: The Good Parts
events.summary: Douglas Crockford's book title became a rallying cry — use the small subset of JavaScript that is reliable and ignore the rest.
events.about: In 2008 many teams treated JS as a toy language. Crockford argued you could write serious software by deliberately avoiding the bad parts — influencing lint rules, style guides, and later [TypeScript]'s stricter subsets.

narrative.whyChosen: The title that legitimized JavaScript as a professional language.
narrative.whyImportant: It gave teams permission to subset the language instead of using all of it.
narrative.problemSolved: Developers lacked a shared guide for which JS features were safe in production.

events.title: Google App Engine opens to all developers
events.summary: Google opened [App Engine] sign-ups to everyone on May 28, 2008 at [Google I/O] — ending the invite-only preview that began in April.
events.about: After 150,000 developers joined the waitlist, [App Engine] became publicly available with pricing tiers and new APIs — [Python] apps could scale on Google's infrastructure without provisioning servers. It validated PaaS as a category alongside [Heroku] and set expectations for cloud-native deployment.

narrative.whyChosen: Opening [App Engine] proved managed cloud hosting had mass developer demand.
narrative.whyImportant: It moved PaaS from invite-only experiment to a product any developer could try.
narrative.problemSolved: Preview waitlists blocked teams from evaluating Google's platform for real workloads.
